0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Korah] or [the Korahites]

1.note: Here and throughout this psalm, the psalmist is applying the terms **we**, **our**, and **us** to himself and his fellow Judeans but not to God, to whom he is speaking. So use the exclusive forms of those terms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

It might seem that the expression **with our ears** adds extra information to this statement that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you may choose not to represent this expression in your translation. However, it does add some emphasis, and you may also choose to reflect that emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [we have heard] or [we have clearly heard]
See how you translated the term “fathers” in 22:4. Alternate translation: [our forefathers]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the work you did]

The psalmist is using the term **days** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their time]

The **fathers** or ancestors who **recounted** the **work** described in verses 2 and 3 did not experience it personally. The psalmist is using them generally to represent earlier generations of Israelites and specifically to represent the generation that conquered and occupied the land of Canaan. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for the generation that conquered and occupied the land of Canaan]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **antiquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in ancient times]

2.note: The psalmist is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb translated as **you drove out** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what the Israelites did not do, as described in the next verse, and what God did. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You were the one who drove out]
Here, **hand** represents “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by your power]

In each case, the pronoun **them** refers to the “fathers” or ancestors of the Israelites mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but you planted our ancestors … but you sent our ancestors]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually **planted** the Israelites in the land of Canaan, as if they had been plants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you settled our ancestors there]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but you sent them into the land] or [but you sent our ancestors into the land]

While it is true that God **sent** the Israelites into the land of Canaan in the sense that he commanded them to go there, the sense here seems to be that God actively propelled them into the land by helping them. That was in contrast to the way he **caused harm** to the nations he drove out. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be

3.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but a complementary truth by way of concession. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed,] or [Admittedly,]

The psalmist is using one kind of weapon, a **sword**, to mean weapons in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with their weapons] or [militarily]
Here, **arm** represents “power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and their own power]

3.q: כִּֽי־יְמִֽינְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ֭⁠זְרוֹעֲ⁠ךָ וְ⁠א֥וֹר פָּנֶ֗י⁠ךָ כִּ֣י רְצִיתָֽ⁠ם
3.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but your right hand and your arm and the light of your face saved them, for you favored them]

3.q: כִּֽי־יְמִֽינְ⁠ךָ֣ וּ֭⁠זְרוֹעֲ⁠ךָ וְ⁠א֥וֹר פָּנֶ֗י⁠ךָ כִּ֣י רְצִיתָֽ⁠ם
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [but because you favored them, your right hand and your arm and the light of your face saved them]

In this context, the terms **right hand** and **arm** mean similar things, since they both represent power. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [but your very strong power]

The **light** of God’s **face** represents his favor, as if he were smiling and looking brightly at someone. See how you translated the similar expression in 4:6. Alternate translation: [and the favor you showed them]

4.note: The psalmist is stating the pronoun **he** for clarity and emphasis. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You are the one who is my king]
Since the psalmist uses first-person plural pronouns throughout most of this psalm, you may wish to use one here, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [our king]

The psalmist is speaking of the **salvation of Jacob** as if it were a living thing that God could **Command**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Bring about the salvation of Jacob]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Act to save Jacob]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please command]

The psalmist is using the name **Jacob** to represent the Israelite people, who were descendants of a man named Jacob. God gave him the name Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [us Israelites]

5.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelite army were actually a horned animal that would **gore** and **trample** an opposing army as if it were another animal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we push back … we defeat]

In this context, God’s **name** seems to represent his authority. The psalmist seems to mean that since God assigned the land of Canaan to the Israelites, when they fight to defend that territory, they are doing so on his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by your authority]

The psalmist is speaking of the **adversaries** of Israel as if they were physically **arising** to a higher elevation. See how you translated the similar expression in 18:48. Alternate translation: [the ones attacking us]

6.note: As in verse 3, here the word **For** introduces not a reason but a complementary truth. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

6.q: לֹ֣א בְ⁠קַשְׁתִּ֣⁠י אֶבְטָ֑ח וְ֝⁠חַרְבִּ֗⁠י לֹ֣א תוֹשִׁיעֵֽ⁠נִי
6.note: The psalmist is using two kinds of weapons, his **bow** and his **sword**, to mean weapons in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not rely on my weapons, no, those weapons do not save me]

6.q: לֹ֣א בְ⁠קַשְׁתִּ֣⁠י אֶבְטָ֑ח וְ֝⁠חַרְבִּ֗⁠י לֹ֣א תוֹשִׁיעֵֽ⁠נִי
6.note: If you decided to use first-person plural pronouns in verse 4, you may wish to do that here as well. Alternate translation: [We do not trust in our bows, and our swords do not save us] or [We do not rely on our weapons, no, those weapons do not save us]

The psalmist is speaking of his **sword** as if it were a living thing that could **save** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I do not win victories with my sword]

8.note: The psalmist is saying **all of the day** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [continually]

In this context, God’s **name** seems to represent his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and we will praise your reputation] or [and we will praise you for who you are]
See how your translation team decided at 3:2 to represent the term “Selah.”

9.note: The psalmist is speaking as if God would previously **go out** physically with the Israelite **armies**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you no longer help our armies]

10.note: The psalmist may not mean to say that God is actively opposing the Judeans. He may be describing the consequences of God no longer helping them. Alternate translation: [You oblige us to turn back from the enemy]

In this context, the expression **for themselves** has the sense of “as they wish” or “at will,” that is, without any resistance. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at will]

11.note: The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **sheep** that are characterized by being slaughtered and eaten as **food**. In context, the emphasis seems to be on the slaughtering, as the parallel phrase “sheep of slaughter” in verse 22 indicates. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like sheep that are slaughtered]

The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** that people slaughter for **food** are very vulnerable and easily killed, so the Judeans have become very vulnerable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. The point of comparison is the same in verse 22. Alternate translation: [very vulnerable, like sheep that are slaughtered]

12.note: The psalmist means that God has not become greater in terms of wealth. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and you have not increased in wealth]

13.q: תְּשִׂימֵ֣⁠נוּ חֶ֭רְפָּה לִ⁠שְׁכֵנֵ֑י⁠נוּ לַ֥עַג וָ֝⁠קֶ֗לֶס לִ⁠סְבִיבוֹתֵֽי⁠נוּ
13.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, and you have made us a scorn and a derision to the ones around us]

13.q: תְּשִׂימֵ֣⁠נוּ חֶ֭רְפָּה לִ⁠שְׁכֵנֵ֑י⁠נוּ לַ֥עַג וָ֝⁠קֶ֗לֶס לִ⁠סְבִיבוֹתֵֽי⁠נוּ
13.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **reproach**, **scorn**, and **derision**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You have given our neighbors occasion to reproach us, and you have given the ones around us occasion to scorn and deride us]

The psalmist does not mean that God has made the Judeans something that causes **reproach** to their **neighbors**. He means that they have become an object of their neighbors’ reproach. He means the same thing when he uses the terms **scorn** and **derision**. If you retain these abstract nouns in your translation, you could indicate this explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You have made us an object of reproach to our neighbors, an object of scorn and derision]

14.note: In this culture, shaking or wagging one’s head at a person or group was a symbolic action by which people showed contempt and expressed mockery toward that person or group. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a group at which individuals among the peoples shake their heads contemptuously]

15.note: See how you translated the phrase “all of the day” in 44:8. Alternate translation: [My disgrace is continually before me]
If you decided to use first-person plural pronouns in verses 4 and 6, you may wish to do that here as well. Alternate translation: [our disgrace is before us, and the shame of our faces covers us]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **disgrace** were actually an object that was **before** or in front of him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am aware of my disgrace]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **face**, to mean all of him in the act of being ashamed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my shame covers me]

The psalmist is speaking as if **shame** were physically covering him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the shame of my face overwhelms me]

Hebrew culture associated **shame** with the **face**. If your culture does the same thing, you may wish to retain the figurative usage in your translation and express this in terms that the people of your culture would use. Alternate translation: [I have lost face, and shame overwhelms me]

16.note: Here, **face** represents “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

Together, the expressions **an enemy** and **one avenging** express a single idea. The expression **one avenging** tells what kind of **enemy** the psalmist is describing. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a vengeful enemy]

17.note: The psalmist is speaking of the misfortunes he has described as if they were a living thing that could have **come** to the Judeans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [All of this has happened to us]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Judeans might actually have **forgotten** their God, that is, ceased to have remember anything about him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The meaning is similar in verse 20. Alternate translation: [but we have not neglected to worship you]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s **covenant** as if it were a person with whom the Judeans could have **dealt falsely**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we have not dealt falsely with you by not keeping your covenant]

18.note: The psalmist is using one part of the Judeans, their **heart**, to mean all of them in the act of remaining loyal to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have not turned ourselves back]

The term **heart** is singular in form, but it refers to the hearts of all of the Judeans. If you retain the image of the heart, if it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of that word. Alternate translation: [Our hearts have not turned themselves back]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Judeans were physically following God and had not **turned** to go in the opposite direction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We are still loyal to you]

The psalmist is using one part of the Judeans, their **steps**, to mean all of them in the act of remaining loyal to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and we have not turned aside from your way]

The psalmist is speaking as if how God wants people to live were a **way** or path on which people were supposed to walk. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nor have we stopped living as you want us to live]

19.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **a place of jackals** to represent a desolate area where only wild animals live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [so that our land is now desolate]

The term **jackals** describes wild dogs that live in desolate regions. If your readers would not be familiar with what a jackal is, in your translation you could use the name of a similar animal that your readers would recognize, or you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [wild dogs]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually **covered** the Judeans with a **dark shadow**. He means that God has allowed them to be in a situation in which they are in great danger of death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have brought us into a situation of mortal peril]

20.q: אִם־שָׁ֭כַחְנוּ שֵׁ֣ם אֱלֹהֵ֑י⁠נוּ וַ⁠נִּפְרֹ֥שׂ כַּ֝פֵּ֗י⁠נוּ לְ⁠אֵ֣ל זָֽר׃ הֲ⁠לֹ֣א אֱ֭לֹהִים יַֽחֲקָר־זֹ֑את כִּֽי־ה֥וּא יֹ֝דֵ֗עַ תַּעֲלֻמ֥וֹת לֵֽב
20.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 44:20 and 44:21 into a verse bridge and put the last phrase in verse 21 at the beginning of verse 20, since it gives the reason for the result that the material in the rest of these verses describes. Alternate translation: [Since our God knows the secrets of the heart, if we had forgotten his name and spread out our palms to a foreign god, would he not have discovered this?]

In this context, **the name of our God** represents calling on God by name. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [If we had ceased to call on our God by name] or [If we had ceased to worship our God explicitly]

The psalmist is using the action of spreading out one’s **palms** toward the sky to represent prayer, since that was the characteristic posture of prayer in this culture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and prayed]

21.note: The psalmist is using the question form to make a strong affirmation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God would certainly have discovered this!]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s private thoughts and memories. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the things that people do but do not tell others about]

22.note: The expression **are killed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [our enemies are killing us]
See how you translated the same expression in 44:8. Alternate translation: [continually]

The expression **are considered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [our enemies consider us]

23.note: The psalmist is using the question form as a rebuke. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Awake! You should not be sleeping, Lord! Wake up!]

The psalmist is speaking as if God were actually **sleeping** and therefore unaware of or unconcerned about the Judeans’ situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action! You should not do nothing while we are in such danger! Help us!]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. (By contrast, the imperatives **Awake** and **Wake up** are urgent summonses rather than requests.) Use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Please do not reject us]

24.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Why do you hide your face, and why do you forget our affliction and our oppression]

As in the previous verse, the psalmist is using the question form as a rebuke. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not hide your face, and you should not forget our affliction and our oppression!]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had actually hidden his **face** so that the Judeans could not see it. He means that it is as if God had turned his face away from the Judeans rather than looking at them with a bright expression that indicated favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you not regard us with favor] or [Please regard us with favor, and do not forget]

The psalmist is speaking as if God had once known about the **affliction** and **oppression** of the Judeans but had now forgotten about them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [neglect to do anything about]

25.note: Here the psalmist is using the word **For** to introduce a reason why God should help the Judeans. Alternate translation: [Help us because]

25.q: שָׁ֣חָה לֶ⁠עָפָ֣ר נַפְשֵׁ֑⁠נוּ דָּבְקָ֖ה לָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ בִּטְנֵֽ⁠נוּ
25.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the Judeans had physically fallen onto the **earth** and could not get up and as if their **soul** or inner being had similarly **sunk down into the dust**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We have no physical strength left, as if we had fallen down and could not get up, and we have no strength in our inner beings either, as if they had collapsed into the dust]

In this verse, the words **soul** and **belly** are singular in form, but they refer to the souls and bellies of all of the Judeans. If you retain the images that the psalmist is using, if it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of these words. Alternate translation: [our souls have sunk … our bellies cling]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **belly**, to mean all of him in the act of clinging to the **earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our bodies cling to the earth]

The psalmist is speaking as if each Judean’s **belly** or body were actually clinging to the **earth**. He means that it is as if each Judean had fallen and could not get up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our bodies have fallen to the earth and we cannot get up]

26.q: ק֭וּמָֽ⁠ה עֶזְרָ֣תָ⁠ה לָּ֑⁠נוּ וּ֝⁠פְדֵ֗⁠נוּ לְמַ֣עַן חַסְדֶּֽ⁠ךָ
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [because of your covenant faithfulness, arise as a helper to us and redeem us]

The psalmist assumes that God will understand that by **Arise**, he means “Take action.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Take action]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please take action]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in order to be faithful to your covenant]
